entry.assertion: Standard Western dietary pattern is associated with significantly lower gut microbiome alpha diversity compared to Flexitarian (Faith's PD: P=0.009; observed ASVs: P=0.007) and Health-Conscious Western (Faith's PD: P=0.048) patterns. Data-driven dietary patterns (DP5) explained more microbiome beta-diversity variance than any individual nutrient or a priori diet index (P ≤ 0.0002).

Baseline Prevotella abundance predicts weight loss in response to a high-fiber/whole grain diet. In a 6-week RCT (n=75 overweight adults), high-Prevotella subjects lost nearly 2 kg more on a whole grain diet compared to refined wheat, while low-Prevotella subjects remained weight-stable. Participants with no detectable Prevotella (0-P group) gained weight on refined wheat but lost weight on whole grain (P=0.009), and showed greater waist circumference reduction (−4.7 vs +0.8 cm, P<0.05).

Aerobic 'disruptor taxa' in the duodenum — Klebsiella, Escherichia-Shigella, Enterococcus, Clostridium (C. perfringens by V4 classification), Romboutsia, Aeromonas, and Bacteroides — displace strict anaerobes (Porphyromonas, Leptotrichia, Prevotella, Neisseria) when present, creating a mutually exclusive ecological pattern. The disruptor taxa axis (PC2) correlates with patient-reported GI symptom scores: bloating, incomplete evacuation, and constipation showed the highest correlation, while urgency, excess gas, and diarrhea were weaker. Serum IL-8 showed a weak positive correlation with the disruptor taxa axis.

In a double-blind RCT of 40 sedentary women (BMI 25-40, age 18-45), 6 weeks of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) combined with FOS-enriched inulin (12 g/d) vs HIIT + placebo (maltodextrin 12 g/d) produced differential gut microbiome responses. The primary endpoint (VO2peak) was not significantly different between groups (P=0.58). However, HIIT-Inulin produced a 38-fold increase in Bifidobacterium (FDR<0.05), with significant increases in Actinobacteria and Bifidobacteriaceae relative to HIIT-Placebo. HIIT-Inulin also improved ventilatory thresholds: VT1 (+4.3%) and VT2 (+4.2%) vs placebo (P<0.05). In exploratory analysis, higher VO2peak responders (regardless of group) had 9.4x Bacteroides_A abundance (P<0.0001, FDR=0.12), 2.2x B. uniformis (P<0.001, FDR=0.08), 2.2x gellan degradation pathways (P<0.00001, FDR<0.05), and higher fecal SCFAs (+14.4 μmol/g, P=0.049 unadjusted, P=0.13 after covariate adjustment).

AI-personalised diet (PD) significantly increased Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance (P<10^-4, paired t-test) while low-FODMAP diet did not (P>0.05) over 6 weeks in IBS patients. PD also significantly decreased Ruminococcaceae family abundance (P<10^-5), with no change in FODMAP group. Alpha diversity showed significant shifts in PD group but not FODMAP. Beta diversity (Bray-Curtis PERMANOVA) shifted significantly in both groups for IBS-C and IBS-M subtypes (P<0.05), with PD showing more pronounced shifts and lower P values. IBS-D subgroup did not achieve significant beta-diversity shifts in either group.

A low FODMAP diet does not alter total fecal SCFA concentration compared to control diets in IBS patients (meta-analysis: SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.63 to 0.13, P=0.20, n=208 across 4 trials). Individual SCFAs (acetate, propionate, butyrate, valerate) and fecal pH also showed no significant differences.

Habitual dietary FODMAP intake inversely correlates with breath hydrogen (BH₂) response to an inulin challenge over 24 hours (Pearson r = −0.42, P = 0.009, n = 17). Higher habitual FODMAP consumers produce less BH₂ from an inulin bolus, suggesting their microbiome is better adapted to ferment FODMAPs efficiently (toward SCFAs rather than gas). This correlation held across both PI and control arms combined.

Breath volatile metabolites (BVM) measured by SIFT-MS can detect and discriminate fiber fermentation in real-time. After single ingestion of chitin-glucan (4.5g, fermentable insoluble fiber) vs maltodextrin (non-fermentable control) in 15 healthy H₂-producing volunteers: (1) Exhaled butyric acid significantly increased after CG, peaking at 6h postprandial (P<0.05, Wilcoxon); (2) Six additional BVM discriminated CG vs maltodextrin: triethylamine, 2,3-butanedione, 3-hydroxybutanone, pentane, methanol, ethane (repeated measures ANOVA P<0.05); (3) 13 MS-fragments from untargeted analysis discriminated CG vs maltodextrin at 6h by PLS-DA (Monte Carlo P=0.001); (4) Baseline Mitsuokella abundance was the sole genus correlating with exhaled butyrate net AUC after CG; (5) Standard breath H₂ and CH₄ were NOT significantly different between CG and maltodextrin, suggesting BVM provides information beyond traditional lactulose breath testing.

Roseburia spp. perform dual metabolic functions: they ferment dietary fibers to produce butyrate and they metabolize linoleic acid (18:2n-6) via conjugation, linking SCFA production to fatty acid transformation within the same organism.

Twelve sugar pyruvate fermentation pathways and mixed acid fermentation are enriched in the duodenal microbiome of SIBO subjects (≥10³ CFU/mL on MAC) compared to non-SIBO (FC >1.1, adjusted P<.05). Aerobic cleavage of pyruvate is also enriched, including pyruvate to cytochrome bd/bo oxidase electron transfer (FC=1.48, adjusted P=2.09E-09). These pathways correlated with diarrhea (r=0.252, P=.0034), bloating (r=0.185, P=.025), urgency (r=0.205, P=.0146), and abdominal pain (r=0.300, P=.0006). Enterobacteriaceae species produce H₂ from sugar fermentation, and microbial reactions known to produce or consume H₂ are largely represented by pyruvate fermentation coupled with aerobic/anaerobic respiration.

The 4-SURE diet combines four strategies to reduce colonic sulfide: (1) increase fermentable fiber to 10-15g/d resistant starch + 5g/d slowly fermentable NSP, (2) restrict total protein to <=1.2g/kg/d, (3) restrict sulfur-containing amino acids to <=1.5-2.0g/d, (4) avoid sulfite/sulfate/nitrate/carrageenan food additives.
On the 4-SURE diet, fiber intake increased from 21.5 to 34.4 g/d (P<0.0001), resistant starch from 2.84 to 12.6 g/d (P<0.0001), while inorganic sulfur fell by 24% from 1.34 to 1.02 g/d (P=0.042).

Insoluble fiber intake is positively associated with relative abundance of Faecalibacterium (β=0.28, 95% CI: 0.03–0.52, P=0.02) and Coprococcus (β=0.28, 95% CI: 0.03–0.38, P=0.03), both known butyrate-producing genera.

Total fiber intake is positively associated with Blautia abundance (β=0.29, 95% CI: 0.14–0.43, P≤0.001) and with multiple butyrate-associated genera including Dorea, Oscillospira, and Coprococcus, while higher total sugar is associated with lower Bacteroides and Lachnospiraceae-Clostridium.

Walnut consumption (42 g/d for 3 weeks) significantly increased relative abundance of butyrate-producing Firmicutes including Faecalibacterium (0.79→2.77%, P=0.02), Roseburia (1.45→1.32%→significant increase P<0.01), and Clostridium (0.72→1.07%, P=0.01), while reducing Ruminococcus, Dorea, Oscillospira, and Bifidobacterium (all P<0.05).

A low FODMAP diet consistently reduces Bifidobacteria abundance in IBS patients, with lower levels observed both between-group (vs control diets) and within-group (vs baseline) across 7 of 9 included RCTs (n=403 total). This 'antibifidogenic' effect is the most consistent microbiome change from FODMAP restriction.

Soluble corn fiber (SCF, PROMITOR SCF 85) dose-dependently increases Parabacteroides proportions in the fecal microbiome: 1.1% at 0g, 2.1% at 10g/d, 3.0% at 20g/d (P<0.001 for 0 vs 20g/d). SCF also increases alpha diversity (Chao1: 1104→1402→1282 for 0/10/20g, P<0.05) and lowers fecal pH at highest dose (P<0.02).

An Exclusion diet pattern (low-carbohydrate, modified paleo) is associated with a 3-to-6-fold reduction in Bifidobacterium relative abundance compared to all other dietary patterns (P ≤ 1.2 × 10⁻⁷). Bifidobacterium depletion persists after adjusting for carbohydrate percentage, fat percentage, and health conditions, and is better explained by overall diet pattern than by any single nutrient.

Psyllium (PI) co-administered with inulin reduces early breath hydrogen (BH₂ 0-6h AUC) by shifting fermentation to a later colonic time window. Both PI and divided-dose inulin (DDI) significantly reduced BH₂ 0-6h vs control (PI: −8.99 [−13.33 to −4.64], P<0.0001; DDI: −10.86 [−15.18 to −6.54], P<0.0001). However, DDI increased BH₂ 6-12h (27.93, P<0.0001) and 12-24h (35.61, P<0.0001), while PI only increased BH₂ 12-24h (22.49, P=0.0002). PI acts by delaying inulin delivery to the colon via viscous gel formation, not by reducing total fermentation. Total 24h BH₂ AUC was not significantly reduced by PI vs control (P=0.32).

Supplementation with 21 g/d of poorly digested soluble fibers (polydextrose or soluble corn fiber) for 21 days shifted the fecal Bacteroidetes:Firmicutes ratio in healthy men (n=21, crossover RCT). Firmicutes decreased from 68% (no-fiber control) to 56% (polydextrose) and 55% (SCF) (P<0.001). Bacteroidetes increased from 25% to 36% and 38% respectively (P<0.001). The B:F ratio correlated positively with total dietary fiber intake (r=0.45, P=0.003) but NOT with BMI (r=0.06, P=0.64). Parabacteroides was the primary driver, increasing 4-5× (1.66%→6.83% PDX, 7.94% SCF, P<0.001). However, known butyrate producers Eubacterium (11.2%→6.31% PDX, 5.94% SCF), Dorea (1.32%→0.81% PDX, 0.82% SCF), and Roseburia (3.80%→2.33/2.40% SCF) all DECREASED with fiber (P<0.001). Butanoate metabolism genes were depleted 15-20% (P=0.001, q=0.004). Amino acid metabolism genes showed the largest functional enrichment after fiber (P<0.0001).

In 303 older men (age 71±4, BMI 25.2±3.6) from the Harvard MLVS with 911 fecal metagenomes (shotgun sequencing), higher healthy plant-based diet index (hPDI) was significantly associated with: enrichment of Bacteroides cellulosilyticus and Eubacterium eligens; amino acid biosynthesis pathways (L-isoleucine, L-valine) and pyruvate fermentation to isobutanol; lower triglycerides (-8.9 mg/dL per SD hPDI), lower HbA1c (-0.06%), lower BMI (-0.9 kg/m²), and lower metabolic risk score (-1.0 unit per SD). Critically, the hPDI-metabolic benefit was modulated by gut microbiome composition: the benefit was more pronounced with higher B. uniformis and lower Prevotella copri. P. copri carriers showed attenuated hPDI-metabolic associations (P-interaction <0.01). Clostridium clostridioforme enhanced and Blautia hydrogenotrophica attenuated the hPDI-metabolic score association.

Four-week low-FODMAP diet reduced fecal SCFA abundance by >50% specifically in IBS-P metabotype patients (n=18): acetic acid (p<0.0001, q<0.05), propanoic acid (p<0.0001, q<0.05), butanoic acid (p<0.05, q<0.1) all significantly reduced (Wilcoxon signed rank). Branched-chain SCFAs (2-methylpropanoic, 2-methylbutanoic, 3-methylbutanoic acid) also reduced but did not survive FDR correction. In IBS-H metabotype (n=21), NO significant changes in any SCFAs or branched-SCFAs after FODMAP restriction. After FODMAP reintroduction at week 16, IBS-P SCFA abundance recalibrated toward levels seen in IBS-H and healthy controls — not depleted, but normalised.

In a multicenter RCT (n=121), AI-personalised diet (ENBIOSIS platform, microbiome-based food scoring) and low-FODMAP diet produced comparable overall IBS-SSS reduction (PD -112.7 vs FODMAP -99.9, P=0.29 between groups). However, in IBS-D subtype specifically, PD achieved significantly greater improvement (IBS-SSS P=0.010, Cohen's d=0.81 large effect) while FODMAP did not reach significance (P=0.312). Both diets effective in IBS-C (both P<0.001) and IBS-M (both P<0.001). PD led to significant improvements in IBS-QOL across all subtypes; FODMAP only in IBS-C and IBS-D. PD also improved HADS anxiety (P<0.001) and depression (P=0.02). Dietary overlap between PD and FODMAP was moderate (Jaccard index 0.29).

PED significantly improved bloating (-43%, P<.001), distention (-40%, P<.001), flatulence (-42%, P<.001), abdominal discomfort (-30%, P=.02), and constipation (-25%, P=.036) during the 2-week diet phase compared to screening in IMO/SIBO subjects; 83% reported adequate global symptom relief.

In SIBO subjects (>=10^3 CFU/mL on MAC), specific bacterial strains show distinct symptom correlation profiles. E. coli BL21(DE3): abdominal pain r=0.284 (P=.049), diarrhea r=0.321 (P=.02), bloating r=0.110 (sig). E. coli K-12: abdominal pain r=0.337 (sig), diarrhea r=0.298 (sig), excess gas r=0.348 (sig), urgency r=0.374 (sig). K. aerogenes KCTC 2190: abdominal pain r=0.374 (P=.013), diarrhea r=0.305 (P=.038), excess gas r=0.286 (P=.048). Escherichia is more associated with bloating and diarrhea; Klebsiella has a greater association with abdominal pain.

Fasting exhaled methane >=10 ppm (IMO-positive) is associated with significantly higher constipation scores (5.65+/-3.47 vs 4.32+/-3.62, P=0.008), higher gas/bloating scores (6.27+/-2.77 vs 5.41+/-2.98, P=0.003), and LOWER diarrhea scores (3.68+/-3.49 vs 4.38+/-3.46, P=0.04) compared to methane-negative subjects (n=732). This confirms the methane-constipation link and the inverse methane-diarrhea relationship at the population level, consistent with methane's known effect of slowing gut transit.

In a meta-analysis of 19 studies (1293 IMO patients vs 3208 controls), intestinal methanogen overgrowth (IMO) is associated with increased constipation (47% vs 38%, OR 2.04, SMD 0.77), decreased diarrhea (37% vs 52%, OR 0.58, SMD -0.71), and decreased nausea (32% vs 45%, OR 0.75). Bloating was reported in 78%, abdominal pain in 65%, and flatulence in 56% of IMO patients. Methane production correlates with slowed intestinal transit, not just stool frequency.

In 30 SIBO/IMO patients completing 2-week PED + 2-week food reintroduction, 83% (25/30) reported adequate global relief at trial end. At reintroduction vs screening: bloating -40% (FDR P<0.001), distention -37% (FDR P<0.001), discomfort -41% (FDR P<0.001), diarrhea -82% (FDR P=0.001), constipation -50% (FDR P=0.005), flatulence -34% (FDR P=0.008), pain -41% (FDR P=0.002), fatigue -34% (FDR P=0.001), urgency -38% (FDR P=0.024), brain fog -68% (FDR P=0.008). During PED itself, diarrhea transiently worsened (+135%, P=0.001) before resolving at reintroduction. Stool looseness increased during PED (expected from liquid diet) but normalized; Bristol 3-5 stools increased from 56% to 71% at trial end (P=0.35).

IBS-P metabotype patients achieved significantly greater symptom improvement from low-FODMAP diet than IBS-H patients. IBS-SSS mean delta: IBS-P 193.8 [56.9%] vs IBS-H 119.6 [39.6%] (p<0.05, independent samples t-test, Cohen's d 0.722). Pain composite score delta: IBS-P 79.5 [63.1%] vs IBS-H 42.1 [38.1%] (p<0.05, Cohen's d 0.689). Remission rate (IBS-SSS <75): IBS-P 43.8% vs IBS-H 25.0% (OR 2.30, 95% CI 1.26-4.21, p<0.005). Both groups improved significantly within-group, but IBS-P response magnitude was approximately double. No significant difference in response between IBS-D vs IBS-M subtypes.

IBS-Diarrhea patients show differential dietary treatment response: AI-personalised diet (PD) achieved significant IBS-SSS improvement (P=0.010, Cohen's d=0.81) while low-FODMAP diet did not reach significance in IBS-D (P=0.312). In contrast, both diets were effective for IBS-C (both P<0.001) and IBS-M (both P<0.001). For IBS-D, stool frequency decreased from 7.13 to 5.09/day in PD group (P=0.70 between groups). This subtype-specific differential suggests that diarrhea-predominant IBS may require microbiome-personalised dietary approaches rather than one-size-fits-all FODMAP restriction.

In the largest synbiotic-bloating RCT to date (n=350 randomized, 219 analyzed at week 6), a 24-strain multi-species synbiotic (DS-01: 53.6 billion AFU including Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus species + 400mg pomegranate extract as polyphenol prebiotic) significantly improved GI quality-of-life (DQLQ 0.80 vs 1.20, P<0.05, 81.4% vs 72.1% improvement), bloating and gas (PROMIS-GI 13a 16.0 vs 21.0, P<0.01; 72.3% vs 55.9% never/rarely bloating, P<0.001), abdominal discomfort (PROMIS-GI 5a 8.0 vs 10.0, P<0.01), constipation (79.2% vs 71.8% no/slight, P<0.05), and bowel regularity (49.5% vs 34.2% moderate-significant improvement, P<0.05) compared to placebo over 6 weeks in otherwise healthy adults with self-reported bloating/indigestion. No significant differences in anxiety, depression, or libido in overall population. No serious adverse events.

An 8-week double-blind RCT in 56 Rome IV-diagnosed IBS females found that Lab4 multistrain probiotic (L. acidophilus CUL60 + CUL21, B. bifidum CUL20, B. animalis subsp. lactis CUL34; 25 billion CFU/day) produced an 85-point between-group IBS-SSS reduction at day 56 (P<0.0001), with 63% achieving >=50-point responder status vs 4% placebo (P<0.0001). All five IBS-SSS subdomains improved significantly: abdominal pain severity (-19.2, P<0.0001), days with pain (-13.6, P<0.0001), bloating severity (P<0.0001), bowel habit dissatisfaction (P<0.0001), and IBS impact on everyday life (-15.7, P<0.0001). Additionally, anxiety (HADS-A: -1.85, P=0.0002; 31.4% reduction), depression (HADS-D: -2.36, P<0.0001; 33.9% reduction), and avoidance/control behaviors (IBS-BRQ: -7.49, P=0.0002) all improved significantly. Normal stool form proportion increased (78% vs 67%, P=0.0106) and loose stools decreased (15.7% vs 24.4%, P=0.0311). No change in alpha diversity, but Roseburia and Holdemanella enriched in probiotic group. No adverse events. Notably, placebo response was only 4% — unusually low for IBS trials, attributed to minimal patient-physician contact (2 visits only).

returned.assertion: Duodenal total microbial load measured by digital PCR spans nearly 5 orders of magnitude (from ~5×10³ to ~10⁹ rRNA gene copies/mL), with a log-normal distribution (mean=10^6.13, SD=1.12 log10 copies/mL). SIBO samples are enriched in specific 'disruptor taxa' (Enterobacteriaceae, Escherichia-Shigella, Clostridium perfringens) rather than showing uniformly higher total microbial load. Disruptor taxa load classification agrees 80% with gold-standard aerobic aspirate culture for SIBO diagnosis. Neither age, gender, PPI use, probiotic intake, nor smoking correlated with total microbial load.

A 5-VOC fecal biomarker model (methylsulfanylmethane, methyldisulfanylmethane, methyltrisulfanylmethane, acetic acid, propanoic acid) predicted IBS microbial subtype (IBS-P vs IBS-H) with AUROC 0.797 (95% CI 0.78-0.94 sensitivity, 0.55-0.88 specificity), sensitivity 78.6%, specificity 71.4% using logistic regression with 10-fold cross-validation. The model combines 3 organosulphur VOCs (elevated in IBS-H) with 2 SCFAs (elevated in IBS-P). Notably, the discriminating VOCs span both metabotypes: organosulphurs as IBS-H markers and SCFAs as IBS-P markers, creating a push-pull classification.

Methane (CH₄) produced by M. smithii has been directly linked to slowing intestinal transit and augmenting small intestinal contractile activity, contributing to constipation. In contrast, H₂S acts as a smooth muscle relaxant through inhibition of L-type calcium channels and BKCa channels, promoting diarrhea. These divergent gas-mediated mechanisms explain the opposing stool phenotypes in IBS-C vs IBS-D.
